description: Question: why does a distant earthquake sway tall towers while low houses next to them barely notice, and why does the nearby one do the opposite? Data: USGS ShakeMap's station list for the M7.1 Ridgecrest, California earthquake of 6 July 2019 (event ci38457511, Caltech/USGS Southern California Seismic Network version): for about 900 strong-motion and broadband stations, the peak ground acceleration (PGA) and the pseudo-spectral acceleration SA at 0.3, 1 and 3 seconds per channel, with the distance to the rupture. USGS data is public domain. Idea: the response spectrum and resonance. A building is, to first order, a damped oscillator (a single degree of freedom) with a natural period of about N/10 seconds for N storeys. SA(T) is the peak acceleration a 5%-damped oscillator of period T reaches in the recorded shaking; SA(T)/PGA is how much it amplifies the ground. Steady shaking at its own period would amplify it 1/2ζ = 10 times; an earthquake's few seconds of broadband motion give about 2–2.5. Steps (Polars and SQL): the nested station list to one row per channel and measure; per station the larger horizontal value of each measure; the spectrum as rows; the median shape SA/PGA per distance bin; attenuation per period (ln(SA·r) on r, giving κ and the distance over which each period's shaking halves); the long-to-short ratio SA(3 s)/SA(0.3 s) against distance; the oscillator's theoretical amplification for 2, 5 and 20% damping. The aha: within 50 km a 0.3 s oscillator (a 3-storey house) feels 2.05 times the ground's acceleration and a 3 s one (a 30-storey tower) 0.24 times; at 400–550 km the numbers are 1.41 and 1.10, and the ratio SA(3 s)/SA(0.3 s) grows by a factor of 1.57 per 100 km (845 stations, r = 0.56). Short-period shaking halves every 77 km, 3 s shaking every 157 km. Near the fault the spectrum peaks at short periods (stiff, low buildings are hit hardest); far away the short periods have been absorbed (rock absorbs a fixed share per cycle, and short periods make more cycles per kilometre), so the spectrum shifts to long periods: tall buildings, long bridges and oil tanks feel distant earthquakes the most. Caveats: three periods only (ShakeMap 3 station lists); the 0 s point is PGA; site conditions (the Los Angeles basin amplifies long periods) and directivity along the rupture add scatter; distance is to the rupture as ShakeMap estimated it; the attenuation fit assumes 1/r spreading at all distances (long-period surface waves spread more slowly), so κ is an apparent value, good for comparing periods, not a material Q; stations below 0.02 %g PGA and beyond 550 km are dropped. Next: compare a smaller quake (the M6.4 foreshock, ci38443183) to see magnitude shift the spectrum, or join each station's Vs30 (site stiffness) to separate site from distance.
name: Response spectra: which buildings an earthquake shakes
